fields.meaning: Relying on…, with the help of…
examples: I headed for my destination, relying on a map.
I walked along the mountain path by the light of a flashlight.
Relying on my memory, I'm looking for an old friend.
I relied on a friend and had them introduce me to a job.
I have worked hard up to now, relying on my father's words.
I found a business partner by relying on my connections.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes “relying/leaning on” rather than an objective rule; a personal, situational nuance.
Often used with verbs of motion/searching/resolving actions:行く,探す,見つける,進む.
“～を頼りとして” is formal, with a written-language style; “～を頼りにして” emphasizes an ongoing state.

• Relying on N as a clue, means, or support to carry out an action.
• Often implies that N is not perfect but is something you can cling to in a difficult situation.
• Used for both concrete things (杖, 地図, 明かり) and abstract ones (記憶, 縁, 伝手, 言葉).
fields.notes:
• Often used with vague “clues”: 手がかり, 記憶, 伝手, 当て.
• Can imply a feeling of weakness/needing something to cling to, creating a literary nuance.
• In polite communication, “ご縁を頼りに” sounds humble. | Variant: ～を頼りにして
mistakes: Confusing it with ～をもとに/～に基づいて: these two patterns emphasize a firm basis and do not carry the nuance of “clinging to”.
Using it with a subject that cannot be a “support”: a noun that is too abstract cannot serve as a concrete clue → the sentence becomes vague.
Wrong particle direction: it must be を頼りに (not に頼りに).

examples: We will make use of this temple as a tourism resource.
We will have him attend the meeting as our representative.
I promoted my experience as a strength.
We drew a conclusion using the data as evidence.
We should protect water as the source of life.
You should fulfill your responsibilities as a student.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes role/function rather than essential nature. When you want to define the essential nature, consider ～という.
In expository writing: often used with abstract nouns such as目的/手段/基準/対象/材料/資源/代表.
Polite style, suitable for reports and plans: ～を～として活用/位置づける/採用/設定.

• N1をN2として: regard/place/position N1 in the capacity/role/purpose of N2.
• Used to indicate: a role (代表/責任者), a function (材料/手段/目的), a standard/basis (根拠/基準).
• Nuance: somewhat formal, often found in written language, presentations, and descriptions of function.
• Different from にとって: ～として means “in the capacity of/role”, not “for (a viewpoint, benefit)”.
fields.notes:
• N2 is usually an abstract noun indicating a role: 目的/基準/根拠/立場/象徴/題材/条件/前提.
• In advertising/PR: ～を強みとして/特徴としてアピールする is a very common pattern.
• Inversion to emphasize N2: N2としてN1を活用する is also found in written language.
meaning_vi: ～を・・・にする/と考(かんが)える/と決(き)める
Take... as..., decide
examples: 1. 今年1年、大学降格を目標としてがんばるつもりだ。
This year, I plan to work hard with getting into university as my goal.
2. 大学で遺文交流をとしてサークルを作った。
We set up a club at the university with the purpose of intercultural exchange.
3. この奨学金は留学生を対象としたものです。
This scholarship is for international students (it takes international students as its target).
4. 山田氏を団長とする訪米団が結成された。
We formed a delegation to visit the US with Mr. Yamada as its leader.
5. 次の世代のために、一人一人が環境問題を自分の問題としてとらえる必要がある。
For the sake of the next generation, each person needs to regard environmental problems as their own problem. explain: Used when you want to take a noun as the purpose, role, etc. of an action. Before [として] come words indicating purpose, standpoint, role, type… ⏐ examples: 1. この祭りは、住民の社会参加を目的として始められた。
This festival was started with the purpose of residents' participation in society.
2. 山田さんをリーダーとするサークルを作る。
Set up a sports club with Mr. Yamada as its leader.
3. 環境問題をテーマとしたテレビ番組を見る。
a TV program with environmental problems as its theme.
mistakes: Dropping “を” in the double pattern: Incorrect: AとしてB. Correct: AをBとして when you mean “take A as B”.
Confusing it with にとって: “for (a viewpoint)” → にとって; ～として is not used.
Using an N2 that does not fit a role: choose a noun meaning “role/function”; do not use an adjective.
Wrong order: put N1 (the target) first and N2 (the role) after: N1をN2として.

fields.meaning: Should have…, if only I had… (regret over not doing something)
examples: Oh no, I should have left earlier. Then I wouldn't have had to rush like this.

A: You still can't get a hotel?
B: No, everywhere's really crowded. If I'd known it would be like this, I should have booked earlier.
fields.notes: A spoken-language form of 「のだった」.

fields.meaning:
～の面(めん)で、～の見地(けんち)から
From the standpoint of
examples: ・for religious reasons ・money-related trouble ・in form ・because of one's position
Legally, men and women are equal, but in reality there is still a lot of discrimination.
In theory, the experiment should have succeeded, but it failed. I wonder why.
When the offender is a child, both the police and the media are required to show educational consideration.
That couple seems to get along on the surface (= in appearance), but apparently that's not really the case.

fields.name: ～上（で）（in terms of・scope）
fields.meaning:
～の面(めん)で、～の範囲(はんい)で
In, within the scope of
examples: I only have a work relationship with him.
On the map it looked close, but when I actually walked there, it was far.
According to the calendar it's already autumn, but the fierce late-summer heat continues.
Mr. Mizuno, a third-generation Japanese descendant, looks no different from a Japanese person, but his way of thinking is completely American.

fields.name: ～とか（hearsay）
examples: I hear tonight's fireworks festival has been canceled because of rain.
I hear the flu is going around right now.
fields.explain:
Used in spoken language.
Carries the sense “I'm not quite sure, but ～” compared with the pattern 「～そうだ」

examples: That is a textbook for beginners.
Production of this product has increased both for the domestic market and for export overseas.
This restaurant's dishes come in small portions and look pretty, so they suit women.
fields.explain:
N向け: takes the noun as the target. Specially made to suit ～.
N向き: right for, suitable for.

examples: As the population increases, resource consumption also increases.
Because the marathon will be held, this road will be closed to traffic.
fields.explain:
Along with one change, another change also takes place. Or events happen simultaneously with each other.
Kanji: 《～に伴う》

examples: There is no problem with using this meeting room on Saturdays and Sundays as well.
It's no problem if you attend in casual clothes.
If you don't mind, could you tell me your age?
We were told that it's no problem even if you're about 5 minutes late.
There is no problem with sharing this document outside the company.
fields.explain:
More formal than構わない,大丈夫; suited to office contexts and regulations.
Often used with ても／でも to express “even if …, there is no problem”.
Can be used in the polite negative form:差し支えありません／ございません.

- Meaning: “there is no obstacle/problem”, “it is fine/OK” in contexts of rules, regulations, and polite communication.
• Used to give permission/agree formally, or to describe that something has no effect.
• Often seen in notices, business emails, instructions, and customer service.
• The question form “差し支えなければ …” is used as a polite opener when asking for private information.
fields.notes:
• Base verb: 差し支える (to cause an obstacle). Adjective form: 差し支えない (no obstacle).
• Commonly used keigo forms: 差し支えございません／差し支えなければ.
• In emails, combine it with 恐れ入りますが／お手数ですが to increase politeness.
mistakes: Used in a casual context, it sounds stiff; choose 構わない/大丈夫 instead.
Confusing who gives permission: only a person with authority should use it to give permission in a notice.
Grammar: dropping も after て/で makes the sentence vague; exams usually require ～ても差し支えない.
Confusing the nuance of 問題ない (judgment) vs 差し支えない (a matter of rules).

fields.connection: 「[sentence/clause]」「それなら(ば) + [judgment/opinion based on that]」（＝じゃ(あ)・それじゃ(あ)）
examples: “I don't want to do that right now.” “Then you don't have to do it.”

“It looks like the roads are really jammed.”
“In that case, let's go by train.”
fields.explain: A conjunction expressing an opinion or conclusion based on a.

fields.meaning:
①～した直後(ちょくご)
Right after doing something
fields.connection: Vた + 矢先に/矢先の / V volitional form + とした + 矢先に
examples: Right after I came to Japan, I left my bag behind somewhere and ended up losing my passport.
Suddenly she said she wanted to break off the engagement. It happened just after we had decided on the wedding venue.
I kept failing no matter how many times I took the exam, and just as I was thinking of giving up, a notice of acceptance arrived.

fields.connection: V/A/N plain form + もの(もん) / V/A/N plain form + んだもの(もん) / Na・N + なんだもの(もん)
examples: I didn't go to the party. I didn't know about it, that's why.
It can't be helped. They're just a kid, after all.
fields.explain:
☞ Expresses a reason that justifies your own position, and is placed at the end of a sentence.
☞ Often used by women and children in conversation.
☞ Often used together with 「だって」
It is sometimes shortened to 「もん」, and both men and women can use it, but the users are young people expressing a reason to justify themselves.

fields.name: ～ものだ・～ものではない（essential nature・exclamation・admonition）
examples: Medicine is bitter by nature.
I really don't want my daughter to do the same job as me.
fields.explain:
（1）Talks about something regarded as natural, common sense
（2）Expresses strong emotion, desire, exclamation, a sigh
* ～もんだ: used in spoken language.

fields.meaning:
①～ようで、～らしく（conjecture）
It seems (conjecture)
fields.connection: V/A plain form + と見えて / ～ように/そうに + 見えて
examples: My father seems to be in a bad mood; he hasn't said a word since morning.
The sweets must have been really delicious; the children ate them all without leaving a single one.
That company seems to be doing well; the lights are on until late at night.
fields.explain:
①～ようで、～らしく（推量(すいりょう)）
It seems (conjecture)

examples: Along with the rise in CO2 concentration in the atmosphere, global warming just keeps advancing.
Because of the weather, vegetable prices just keep going up.
fields.explain:
Expresses that the tendency is ongoing and keeps increasing.
Used with verbs of change.

examples: When it comes to research on Japanese culture, as far as I know, this university is the best.
Telephone calls to inpatients are put through from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. However, this does not apply in emergencies.

fields.name: ～ことに（emotion）
examples: To my surprise, she has divorced and remarried the same person twice.
Interestingly, the house next door and the one next to that both have the same family name as ours.
fields.explain: Placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis, to express feelings and emotions.

fields.meaning: Indicates that ～ is actually the case, but that there is a problem
fields.connection: V/A plain form + (に)は + ～が/けど / ～ことは + ～が/けど (行くには行くが)
examples: It did rain, but only 3 millimeters. This won't solve the water shortage.
“I do understand what you're trying to say, but...”
This tool is convenient, sure, but it's too expensive, so it probably won't sell.
“Did you go to the reunion?” “I did go, but I was coming down with a cold, so I came home after about 30 minutes.”

fields.meaning:
～したくてもできない
Cannot do it even if you want to
fields.connection: V volitional form・Vる + にも + V potential form・Vない or (ない form)
examples: My tooth hurts so much that I can't eat even if I try.
The trains stopped because of the heavy snow, so I couldn't get to school even though I wanted to.
I felt so sluggish that I couldn't get up even if I tried, and ended up taking the day off work.
I've been putting on weight lately, but even if I want to exercise, I have neither the place nor the time.
I want to work, but in this recession I just can't find a job.
I came down with a high fever, but even though I wanted to go to the hospital right away, it was Sunday and everywhere was closed.
fields.notes: It takes the volitional form of a verb, such as 「呼ぼう」「止めよう」, and is followed by an expression with a negative meaning, expressing the meaning “even if you try to do it, you can't.”

fields.meaning: Being just about to ～; being right at the moment of ～ (a literary expression)
fields.connection: (non-volitional V) V volitional form + とする/としている
examples: I was born in 1960, at a time when Japan was about to enter its era of rapid economic growth.
The rocket carrying my wife, an astronaut, is about to be launched right now. All I can do is pray for its success.
The new year is about to begin. I wonder what kind of year this will be.
“As the Olympics come to a close, the Olympic flame, which has burned for 20 days, is now about to go out.”
In the hospital, the exchange between lives about to be born and lives about to fade away is repeated day after day.
I almost fell down the stairs.
I very nearly missed the train.
It was just about to be completed, but then there was a power outage.

fields.meaning: At least…; as for…, doing all one can (だけは)
fields.connection: Vる + だけは + Vた (repeating the same verb)
examples: I did everything I could, so I have no regrets.
Let's at least listen to what they have to say.
I did at least ask, but it was no use.
That's nothing but an excuse.
I'm still only a student, so I lack experience.
No matter how expensive it is, a thing is just a thing.
He visited Japan again.
You must not repeat the same mistake again.
The two met again 10 years later.

fields.meaning: In the manner of…, in the way… (こういうふうに)
fields.connection: どんな あんな こんな どういう + ふうに + V / V plain form
examples: Please write it like this.
How should I explain it?
I wish I could sing like that.
When I warned them, I got scolded instead.
I took the medicine, but I got worse instead.
Cheap things can actually end up costing more.

fields.meaning: Sure enough…, just as expected (果たして)
examples: Sure enough, the result was just as he had predicted.
Will this plan really succeed, I wonder?
When we ran the experiment, sure enough, the hypothesis was correct.

fields.meaning: For the time being, roughly, briefly… (一応)
examples: I did read the explanation, but I still don't really understand it.
I hear it'll be sunny tomorrow, but I'll take an umbrella just in case.
I did graduate from university, for what it's worth.
No one other than authorized personnel may enter.
We're open every day except Sunday.
There's no one other than him who can do this job.
A dog suddenly darted out.
I was suddenly asked a question and couldn't answer.
He suddenly announced that he was quitting the company.

fields.meaning: In one go, in one gulp, all at once… (一気に)
examples: He drank the water down in one gulp.
I ran up the stairs in one go.
Spring came, and the cherry blossoms bloomed all at once.
He's not the so-called genius type.
This is what is known as the spirit of 「おもてなし」.
It's not only the so-called elite who succeed.

fields.meaning: …doesn't mean that… (ことにはならない)
fields.connection: V plain form（including past） + (という) + ことにはならない / Naだ + という / Aい + という
examples: Just because you apologized doesn't mean you've been forgiven.
It doesn't mean that paying money settles everything.
Just participating doesn't mean you've made an effort.

fields.connection: V plain form + の + も当然だ / Vて
examples: After practicing that hard, it's only natural that they would win the championship.
It's only natural that he gets angry.
If you're late every day, it's only natural that you get warned.

fields.meaning: No way…, there's no way that… (ものか/もんか)
examples: That shop? I'll never go there again.
There's no way I'll lose to him.
There's no way this is a coincidence.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: absolutely not ～, not at all ～ ⏐ explain: Expresses strong negation.
「～もんか」、「～もんですか」 are used in spoken language or casual speech. ⏐ examples: 1. あんな店、二度と行くものか。
I will never go to a shop like that again.
2. 元気なもんか。くたくただよ。
Fine? Not at all. I'm exhausted.
3. うれしいもんですか。困っているんです。
How could I be happy? I'm in trouble.

fields.meaning: In the midst of…, while… (雨の中を)
fields.connection: V plain form + 中を 中では / N + の / A
examples: Thank you for taking the trouble to come in the rain.
Thank you for gathering here despite your busy schedules.
You can't read small print in the dark.

fields.meaning: Not having to…, getting by without… (なくて済む)
examples: My friend gave me a ride, so I didn't have to take a taxi.
If you read the manual, you won't have to ask anyone.
Thanks to my insurance, I didn't have to pay for the surgery.
The ship is heading toward the port.
I will keep working hard toward my goal.
The typhoon is moving north.

fields.meaning: Please…, kindly… (お願う/～ようお願いします)
examples: Please wait a moment.
For details, please inquire at the reception desk.
Please fill out this form.
It will probably snow tomorrow.
I think he probably won't come.
The construction will probably continue until next month.
